## Jags
```{r setup, include=FALSE}
#install.packages("rjags")
library(rjags)

```

## 3.9

```{r}
  # Y is num of home runs
  data <- list(regY = 563, regN = 2820, worldY = 10, worldN = 27)

  model_string <- textConnection("model{

   # Likelihood
    regY ~ dpois(regN * lambda1)
    worldY ~ dpois(worldN * lambda2)

   # Priors
    lambda1 ~  dunif(0, 10)
    lambda2 ~  dunif(0, 10)
    ratio <- lambda2/lambda1
 }")

 inits <- list(lambda1 = 0.1,lambda2 = 0.1)
 model <- jags.model(model_string, data = data, inits=inits, n.chains=2, quiet=TRUE)
 update(model, 10000, progress.bar= "none")
 params  <- c("lambda1","lambda2","ratio")
 
 samples <- coda.samples(model, 
            variable.names=params, 
            n.iter=10000, progress.bar= "none")

 
 plot(samples)
 
 summary(samples)
 
 effectiveSize(samples)
 gelman.diag(samples)
 
```

Convergence: The Gel statistic are all exactly 1 and the effective sample sizes are also large (10K+).
The trace plots also look good with a "barcode" shape and don't converge to a single point. All of this points to converging chains.

## 4.1

```{r}
  # Setting up data for jags
  nplace <- ntreat <- 6
  placebo <- c(2.0, -3.1, -1.0, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4)
  treat    <- c(-3.5, -1.6, -4.6, -0.9, -5.1, 0.1)
   
  meanplacebo <- mean(placebo)
  meantreat <- mean(treat)
  
  s2pl   <- mean((placebo - meanplacebo)^2)
  s2trt   <- mean((treat - meantreat)^2)
  sp    <- sqrt((s2pl/2 + s2trt/2))

  postmean <- meantreat - meanplacebo
  postsd <- sp * sqrt( 1/nplace + 1/ntreat)
  credset <- postmean + postsd * qt(c(0.025,0.975), df = nplace + ntreat)

  print(postmean)
  print(postsd)
  print(credset)
```

# Difference
```{r}
  data <- list(n = 6, placebo = placebo, treat = treat)

  model_string <- textConnection("model{

   # Likelihood
   for(i in 1:n){
     placebo[i] ~ dnorm(mu ,tau)
     treat[i] ~ dnorm( mu + delta ,tau)
   }

   # Priors
   mu    ~  dnorm(0, 0.0001)
   delta ~  dnorm(0, 0.0001)
   tau   ~  dgamma(0.1, 0.1)
   sigma <- 1/sqrt(tau)
 }")

 model <- jags.model(model_string, data = data, n.chains = 2, quiet = TRUE)
 update(model, 10000, progress.bar="none")
 params  <- c("delta")
 samples <- coda.samples(model, 
            variable.names=params, 
            n.iter=50000, progress.bar="none")
 summary(samples)

```

Delta is probably negative (quantile shows around 95% of the values for delta are negative). Since
delta is negative that means the treatment succeeds in decreasing the patients' weight.

Changing the prior results in small changes in the data that would not affect the interpretation.
It would simply increase the values' extremity or make it so around 100% of values are negative.

# Sensitive priors
```{r}
  data <- list(n = 6, placebo = placebo, treat = treat)

  model_string <- textConnection("model{

   # Likelihood
   for(i in 1:n){
     placebo[i] ~ dnorm(mu ,tau)
     treat[i] ~ dnorm( mu + delta ,tau)
   }

   # Priors, can change dnorms mean to 1, increase sd. Also can change dgamma shape and scale
   # dnorm: mean: 1,4 0,1
   # dgamma: 1,1 10,10
   mu    ~  dnorm(0, 0.0001)
   delta ~  dnorm(0, 0.0001)
   tau   ~  dgamma(0.1, 0.1)
   sigma <- 1/sqrt(tau)
 }")
 
 model <- jags.model(model_string, data = data, n.chains = 2, quiet = TRUE)
 update(model, 10000, progress.bar="none")
 params  <- c("delta")
 samples <- coda.samples(model, 
            variable.names=params, 
            n.iter=50000, progress.bar="none")
 summary(samples)

```


## 4.2

# Boston Data
```{r}
library(MASS)
data(Boston)
?Boston
```

# More set up
```{r}
# Data setup
crim <- Boston[,1]
zn <- Boston[,2]
indus <- Boston[,3]
chas <- Boston[,4]
nox <- Boston[,5]
rm <- Boston[,6]
age <- Boston[,7]
dis <- Boston[,8]
rad <- Boston[,9]
tax <- Boston[,10]
ptratio <- Boston[,11]
black <- Boston[,12]
lstat <- Boston[,13]
medv <- Boston[,14]
```

# Scaling and na values
```{r}
X <- cbind(crim, zn, indus,
           chas, nox, rm, age, dis, rad,
           tax, ptratio, black,
           lstat, medv)

X <- as.matrix(scale(X))

# Missing data
miss <- is.na(rowSums(X))
X <- X[!miss,]
medv <- medv[!miss]

# Names
vname <- c("Intercept", "crim", "zn", "indus",
           "chas", "nox", "rm", "age", "dis", "rad",
           "tax", "ptratio", "black",
           "lstat", "medv")

n <- length(medv)
p <- ncol(X)
data2 <- list(Y = medv, X = X, n = n, p = p)
params <- c("alpha", "beta")


```

# Jags for 4.2a
```{r}
# Jags
model_string2 <- textConnection("model {

  # Likelihood
  for (i in 1:n) {
    Y[i] ~ dnorm(alpha + inprod(X[i,],beta[]),taue)
  }
  # Priors
    for(j in 1:p){
      beta[j] ~ dnorm(0, 0.001)
    }
    alpha ~ dnorm(0, 0.001)
    taue  ~ dgamma(0.1, 0.1)            
}")

model2 <- jags.model(model_string2, data = data2, n.chains = 2,quiet = TRUE)
update(model2, 10000, progress.bar = "none")
samples2 <- coda.samples(model2, variable.names = params,thin = 10, n.iter = 20000, progress.bar = "none")

sum <- summary(samples2)
rownames(sum$statistics) <- vname
rownames(sum$quantiles)  <- vname
effectiveSize(samples2)
gelman.diag(samples2)
sum

```
Looks like the dist converges as Gel stat is exactly 1 for most and the effect sample size is 1k+, cant graph as the margins are too large.
Could run longer.
The summaries are in the quantiles and means. 

# LM for 4.2b
```{r}
modellm <- lm( medv ~
            scale(crim) + scale(zn) + scale(indus) +
           scale(chas) + scale(nox) + scale(rm) + scale(age) + scale(dis) + scale(rad) +
           scale(tax) + scale(ptratio) + scale(black) +
           scale(lstat), data = data2)
summary(modellm)
```
Results are different .
The Bayesian model attempts to find the best interval for each parameter and estimate a posterior distribution with it. 
While the lm function tries to minimize squares to fit a curve. Should lead to the same results.

# Double exp priors for 4.2c
```{r}
 model_stringbl <- textConnection("model{
   # Likelihood
    for(i in 1:n){
      Y[i] ~ dnorm(alpha+inprod(X[i,],beta[]),taue)
    }
   # Priors
    for(j in 1:p){
      beta[j] ~ ddexp(0,taue*taub)
    }
    alpha ~ dnorm(0,0.001)
    taue  ~ dgamma(0.1, 0.1)
    taub  ~ dgamma(0.1, 0.1)
 }")

model3 <- jags.model(model_stringbl, data = data2, n.chains = 2,quiet = TRUE)
update(model3, 10000, progress.bar = "none")
samples3 <- coda.samples(model3, variable.names = params, thin = 10, n.iter = 20000, progress.bar = "none")


```
# Summary of 4.2c
```{r}
sumbl <- summary(samples3)
rownames(sumbl$statistics) <- vname
rownames(sumbl$quantiles)  <- vname
sumbl
```
The results are smaller, but as the uniformative is close to zero the results aren't too different.
This is different because the BLASSO, BL, model allows for the coef to be set to basically zero, while the gaussian are usually larger.

# Fitting 4.2a again for 4.2d
```{r}
Yo    <- medv[1:500]    # Observed data
Xo    <- X[1:500,]

Yp    <- medv[501:506]     # Counties set aside for prediction
Xp    <- X[501:506,]
no    <- length(Yo)
np    <- length(Yp)
data4 <- list(Yo=Yo,no=no,np=np,p=p,Xo=Xo,Xp=Xp) 

params = c("alpha", "beta", "Yp")
model_string4 <- textConnection("model {

  # Likelihood
  for (i in 1:no) {
    Yo[i] ~ dnorm(alpha + inprod(Xo[i,],beta[]),taue)
  }
  
    # Prediction
  for(i in 1:np){
    Yp[i]  ~ dnorm(mup[i],taue)
    mup[i] <- alpha + inprod(Xp[i,],beta[])
  }
  # Priors
    for(j in 1:p){
      beta[j] ~ dnorm(0, 0.001)
    }
    alpha ~ dnorm(0, 0.001)
    taue  ~ dgamma(0.1, 0.1)            
}")
model4 <- jags.model(model_string4, data = data4, n.chains = 2,quiet = TRUE)
update(model4, 10000, progress.bar = "none")
samples4 <- coda.samples(model4, variable.names = params,thin = 10, n.iter = 20000, progress.bar = "none")

```

# Checking data for s4
```{r}
summary(samples4[,-c(1:np)])
```

# Plotting ppd
```{r}
#Extract the samples for each parameter

 samples4s <- samples4[[1]]
 Yp.samples4s <- samples4s[,1:np] 
 alpha.samples4s <- samples4s[,np+1]
 beta.samples4s <- samples4s[,np+1+1:p]

# Compute the posterior mean for the plug-in predictions  

 beta.mn <- colMeans(beta.samples4s)
 alpha.mn <- mean(alpha.samples4s) 


# Plot the PPD and plug-in

 for(j in 1:6){

    # PPD
    plot(density(Yp.samples4s[,j]))

    # Truth
    abline(v=Yp[j],col=2,lwd=2)

    legend("topright",c("PPD","Truth"),col=1:2,lty=1,inset=0.05)
 }
```
Looks reasonable as the peak of the densities are around of the abline of the true values.
